Read the community history beside the housing authority’s local account and historical charter. The Native Village’s IRA Council and the village corporation are distinct institutions. This small guide introduces selected public histories; it does not represent all Chugach communities or a complete Tatitlek history. Read source annotations for selected pages, dates, perspective and access limits. This is not a complete history or community endorsement.

  1. Tatitlek: From Ancestral Homelands to Modern Challenges

    Begin with the community-specific account of settlement, cultural education and sea relationships.

  2. Tatitlek

    Add the cultural-center history and the explicitly named IRA Council relationship.

  3. Corporate Charter of the Native Village of Tatitlek, Alaska

    Locate the dated organization without confusing approval, ratification and publication dates.

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

A dated organization and older settlement histories

The historical charter printed in 1950 records approval in May 1939 and ratification in December 1946. These dates document the organization, rather than the beginnings of the community. Chugach Alaska Corporation’s local history describes earlier settlement sites and a relocation prompted by mining claims in 1897. Read that account as a Native corporation’s historical interpretation, alongside the primary charter.

Read the sources [3] U.S. Government Printing Office; University of Oklahoma Law Library transcription [1] Chugach Alaska Corporation

02

Language and community learning

Chugach’s account connects Tatitlek’s name with Sugt’stun and describes Peksulineq as an occasion for students, Elders and volunteers to learn and share cultural knowledge. North Pacific Rim Housing Authority adds the opening of the Tatitlek Museum and Cultural Center in 1989, linking it to language and cultural continuity. These are specific educational histories, without an assumption that every tribal citizen participates in the same way.

Read the sources [1] Chugach Alaska Corporation [2] North Pacific Rim Housing Authority

03

Community life beside the sound

The sources place Tatitlek beside Tatitlek Narrows in Prince William Sound. Chugach’s account follows employment at the Ellamar cannery and disruption of fishing and other sea-based livelihoods by the 1989 Exxon Valdez oil spill. This establishes an important coastal relationship while leaving precise harvesting places, present resource conditions and quantified impacts outside this short guide.

Read the sources [1] Chugach Alaska Corporation [2] North Pacific Rim Housing Authority

Tatitlek: From Ancestral Homelands to Modern Challenges ↗

Publication: Undated

A community-specific account of settlement change, the sea and cultural education. The publisher is a Native corporation; its account is not treated as the tribal government speaking. Quantities, current figures and claimed outcomes are omitted.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Tatitlek body paragraphs on place/name, earlier settlement sites, mining-related relocation, Ellamar cannery and the 1989 spill; Quick Facts labels distinguishing village corporation and tribe; Peksulineq cultural-education paragraph. Population, quantities, precise spill distances, continuing impact estimates and photographs not reused.

Review recorded: November 2, 2026

Access note: Specific substantive community body actually read through public web reader, indexed lines 300–331. The linked Tatitlek Corporation history timed out and is not a reviewed source or a separate source count.

Tatitlek ↗

Publication: Undated

A concise local account adding the 1989 opening of the Tatitlek Museum and Cultural Center and the IRA Council relationship. It is used for these historical and institutional points, without adopting current counts or generalizations about every resident.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Complete short main body, lines 6–13: mining/settlement history, IRA Council relationship, access, name, museum/cultural-center opening and earlier regional history. Current council size, precise distances, assertion about all remaining Alutiiq communities and photograph were excluded from the guide.

Review recorded: November 2, 2026

Access note: Public body actually read via web reader; specific museum paragraph confirmed in source body. Linked community-programs page not reviewed.

Corporate Charter of the Native Village of Tatitlek, Alaska ↗

Publication: 1950; approved 1939-05-23; ratified 1946-12-31

A primary historical record whose title, approval and ratification dates must be distinguished. The 1950 imprint preserves a charter approved in 1939 and ratified in 1946; no current legal powers or membership guidance are inferred.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Title/imprint, preamble, purpose/name and management clauses, approval statement and certification of December 31, 1946 ratification. Remaining powers and membership clauses not applied as current law.

Review recorded: November 2, 2026

Access note: Public HTML transcription actually read, indexed lines 7–103. Original printed scan not inspected; transcription scope stated explicitly.
